newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hong Kong shares to gain, then Singapore - SocGen.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong shares to gain, then Singapore - SocGen.

text.p: Hong Kong's stock market is set for more gains in the next few months, but longer term Singapore is likely to be the best equity investment in Southeast Asia, the head of research at SocGen-Crosby Securities said on Thursday.
Manu Bhaskaran told a briefing Hong Kong would see more of the sharp gains it registered in the run-up to its handover to China from Britain on July 1.
The benchmark Hang Seng index could surge 15 percent in the next three months but is then likely to cool off, he said.
Singapore stocks would gain in the second half of the year from an economic recovery after a year of slowdown.

"I think in the short term, Hong Kong will soar. There will continue to be a massive increase in liquidity with interest in red chips (stocks backed by mainland Chinese enterprises) spilling over into blue chips," he said.
"The market could surge 15 percent in the next three months.
"If the blue chips move up as we expect, then we could see the Hang Seng index up to 17,000 within a few months," he said.
"But beyond three months, i.e. the short-term, our recommendation would be neutral."
The Hang Seng closed at 15,055.74 points on Thursday, down 141.05 from Wednesday.
Bhaskaran said he had no doubt Hong Kong would retain its pre-eminence as the most important financial centre in Asia outside Japan.

Its "critical mass" of financial institutions and excellent infrastructure gave it a competitive advantage over all its rivals and this was very unlikely to change just because Beijing had assumed control over the region.

But he said Hong Kong's political discount relative to its neighbours had shrunk to an all-time low and there were bound to be some unpleasant surprises for the markets from the new authorities from time to time.
"There may be too much good news in Hong Kong's pricing," Bhaskaran said.
Singapore's stock market was likely to be a better long-term buy because valuations had tumbled over the last three years in real terms, he said.
The city-state's economy, which has been battered by a slowdown in its core electronics industry over the last 12 months, would recover in the second half of this year.
"Singapore has derated significantly on whatever valuation you look at," he said. "I am fairly confident you will see a significant pick up in economic growth ahead of people's expectations.
"If you believe electronics will recover, (Singapore) will benefit," he said.
He predicted Singapore's gross domestic product (GDP) would grow by 7.3 percent this year after seven percent in 1996, 8.8 percent in 1995 and a double-digit expansion in 1993 and 1994.
The forecast is at the top of economists' forecasts and compares with an official government prediction of five to seven percent GDP growth this year.
A SocGen statement presented at the briefing said Singapore's stock market, as measured by the weighted DBS-50 index, currently had a potential trading range between 470 and 650 points.
The index stood at 502.84 points by 0840 GMT on Thursday.
By the end of 1998, this range would rise to 560 to 780 points, it said.
-- Chris Johnson, Singapore newsroom (65 8703199)
